claims.claim: Praise the specific action or strategy ('you wrote every line of working', 'you checked the sign before moving on'), never the person ('you're clever', 'you're a natural'): in a randomised study of 10-12-year-olds, intelligence praise led children to choose easier tasks, enjoy the work less, persist less after failure and even misreport their scores, while process/effort praise did the opposite.
claims.source_title: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
claims.authors_year: Mueller & Dweck, 1998 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(1), 33-52)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: six experiments, N of roughly 400 fifth-graders in total; after failure, children praised for intelligence showed lower persistence and performance and about 40% misrepresented their scores versus about 10% in the effort-praise group
claims.implication: Add an explicit wording rule to maths-tutor-session, gcse-maths-marker and gcse-spanish-marker: praise = a named action plus why it matters, never an ability label. This targets two logged behaviours directly: the answer-targeting habit and skipping ('I can't'), which are the challenge-avoidance pattern this study produced under person praise.

claims.claim: The parent's own everyday praise style matters over years, not just the tutor's: the proportion of parents' praise that was process-focused when children were toddlers predicted the children's belief that ability can grow and their preference for challenge five years later.
claims.source_title: Parent praise to 1- to 3-year-olds predicts children's motivational frameworks 5 years later
claims.authors_year: Gunderson, Gripshover, Romero, Dweck, Goldin-Meadow & Levine, 2013 (Child Development, 84(5), 1526-1541)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: 53 children observed at home at 14, 26 and 38 months, followed up at 7-8 years; process praise averaged roughly 18% of parents' praise; process-praise proportion, not total praise, predicted incremental beliefs; a later follow-up (Gunderson et al., 2018) linked it to fourth-grade maths and reading achievement
claims.implication: The sample is toddlers, so this is indirect for a 13-year-old, but it supports giving the parent a one-paragraph praise guide (in the progress-report section of gcse-progress-tracker or the dashboard) for when they review a session: comment on what she did ('you kept going on Q4', 'zero blanks again'), not on how able she is.

claims.claim: Avoid inflated praise ('incredible!', 'perfect!', 'amazing work!'): adults give it most to children with low self-esteem, and for exactly those children it increases avoidance of challenging tasks; plain, accurate praise does not.
claims.source_title: "That's not just beautiful—that's incredibly beautiful!": The adverse impact of inflated praise on children with low self-esteem
claims.authors_year: Brummelman, Thomaes, Orobio de Castro, Overbeek & Bushman, 2014 (Psychological Science, 25(3), 728-735)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: three studies of children aged roughly 8-12; in the experiment (Study 3, N about 240), inflated praise led low-self-esteem children to choose the easier of two drawing tasks, while the same praise had the opposite direction of effect for high-self-esteem children
claims.implication: Large language models default to superlatives, and a student with a history of blanks and 'below grade 4' papers is plausibly in the low-self-esteem group this study identified. Write a banned-word list into the skills (no 'amazing', 'perfect', 'incredible', 'brilliant') and require accurate, specific statements in the For-Student marks sheet ('7 of 8 method marks gained on Q3; the one lost was the sign in line 2').

claims.claim: Deliver correction at the task, process or self-regulation level, answering 'what was the goal, what does the work show, what is the next move', and keep praise separate from corrective feedback: feedback aimed at the self (praise, judgements of the person) is the least effective level and can crowd out the useful content.
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: synthesis of prior meta-analyses giving an average feedback effect around d = 0.7 with wide variation by type; it draws on Kluger & DeNisi (1996), whose meta-analysis found roughly one-third of feedback interventions reduced performance, chiefly those directing attention to the self
claims.implication: Make the three questions the template for every correction in maths-tutor-session and for exit-ticket feedback: (1) restate what the question asked, (2) name what her working shows, (3) give the single next move. The marker skills' 'where you lost marks' table and prioritised revision list already follow this shape; the tutor's in-session corrections should too, and should not sandwich corrections between praise sentences.

claims.claim: Feedback is powerful for learning outcomes but weak for motivation and behaviour, and high-information feedback (task plus process plus self-regulation) beats simple right/wrong marking; so expect the Shooting Gallery's correct/incorrect signal to help retrieval, not engagement, and expect richer tutor feedback on recurring errors to do the learning work.
claims.source_title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: 435 studies, 994 effect sizes, overall d = 0.48; larger for cognitive and motor outcomes than for motivational or behavioural ones; high-information feedback around d = 0.99 versus much smaller effects for simple correct/incorrect or reinforcement-style feedback; substantial heterogeneity
claims.implication: The recurring A4 sign and collecting-terms slips across three sessions are exactly where high-information feedback is needed: the tutor should say what happened, why it happens, and give a checking routine, not just mark it wrong. That requires the error pattern to persist between sessions, so the tracker's per-topic 'watch' note should be a structured field the tutor is required to read at session open and update at log time.

claims.claim: Do not build growth-mindset lessons or slogans into the system expecting achievement gains: across meta-analyses the average effect of mindset interventions on achievement is very small and, in the most sceptical recent synthesis, indistinguishable from zero once study quality is accounted for; only cheap, honest framing (errors as information, process praise) is justified.
claims.source_title: To What Extent and Under Which Circumstances Are Growth Mind-Sets Important to Academic Achievement? Two Meta-Analyses
claims.authors_year: Sisk, Burgoyne, Sun, Butler & Macnamara, 2018 (Psychological Science, 29(4), 549-571); see also Macnamara & Burgoyne, 2023 (Psychological Bulletin, 149(3-4), 133-173) and Burnette et al., 2023 (Psychological Bulletin)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: Sisk 2018 mindset-achievement correlation r = 0.10 (273 studies) and intervention effect d = 0.08 (43 studies), with slightly larger effects for academically at-risk and low-SES students; Macnamara & Burgoyne 2023 (63 studies, N about 97,000) reported a very small overall effect that was not reliably above zero after adjusting for study quality and bias; Burnette et al. 2023 reported a small positive effect that depended on targeting and implementation
claims.implication: Spend the student's limited attention on retrieval practice and mastery, not on mindset content. Keep the zero-cost elements (process praise, 'errors are information', no ability labels) and drop any plan for mindset modules, posters or repeated 'your brain can grow' messages in the skills.

claims.claim: A single brief, honest message that struggle in maths is normal and ability grows with practice is worth giving once to a lower-achieving secondary student, because the one large pre-registered trial found a small GPA gain concentrated in lower-achieving students, but the effect was small and context-dependent, so it should be a one-off, not a recurring script.
claims.source_title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: about 12,490 ninth-graders in 65 US schools; two online sessions of roughly 25 minutes; +0.10 grade points in core-course GPA among lower-achieving students, plus higher enrolment in advanced maths; effects depended on peer norms supporting challenge-seeking
claims.implication: Add one scripted moment, for example at the start of the Dec 2026 Foundation mock cycle or after a disappointing paper, where the tutor says plainly that the June 2022 Foundation result reflects unlearned topics, not fixed ability, and shows the evidence (blanks 27/39 marks to zero in five weeks). Do not repeat it every session.

claims.claim: Treat 'I can't', 'skip it', curt replies or sudden quitting as likely emotional dysregulation, not laziness: emotion dysregulation (irritability, low frustration tolerance, rapid escalation) is present in a large minority of children and adolescents with ADHD and is a major driver of impairment, so sessions need a concrete de-escalation routine, not just a hint.
claims.source_title: Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
claims.authors_year: Shaw, Stringaris, Nigg & Leibenluft, 2014 (American Journal of Psychiatry, 171(3), 276-293)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: narrative review; emotion dysregulation reported in roughly 25-45% of children and 30-70% of adults with ADHD depending on definition; three candidate models (core feature, correlated but separate dimension, or a distinct subtype)
claims.implication: The maths-tutor-session rule 'if frustrated pause and suggest a break' needs a trigger and a script: on the second 'skip'/'I can't' in a row, or a one-word reply, the tutor names it neutrally, offers a 5-minute break, then returns with one retrieval item from a secure topic before resuming. Add two fields to tracker_log_session: how the session ended (finished / cut short / walked away) and a 1-5 frustration marker, so the parent can see patterns that today exist only as free text.

claims.claim: 'Rejection sensitive dysphoria' (RSD) is not a validated diagnosis: it is a clinician-coined label (popularised by William Dodson) that appears in neither DSM-5-TR nor ICD-11 and has no validated measurement instrument; the evidence-based constructs behind it are emotional dysregulation in ADHD (C8), rejection sensitivity as a general trait, and comorbid anxiety or depression.
claims.source_title: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) — RSD is absent from its ADHD criteria and specifiers
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); the claim is about absence from DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, which is checkable; recent (2023-2026) scoping reviews of RSD could not be searched for
claims.implication: Do not design around RSD as if it were a diagnosis, and do not use the term in skills or the dashboard. Do design for emotional dysregulation: deliver corrections as matter-of-fact task information (C4), never as a judgement of her, and if intense reactions to correction are frequent the parent should raise it with her clinician rather than self-label.

claims.claim: Parent-teen conflict over academic work in ADHD falls when the parent shifts from control to autonomy support with collaborative goal-setting and monitoring: the STAND programme (parent-teen sessions combining motivational interviewing with organisation, time-management and planning skills) improved parent-rated ADHD symptoms, organisation, homework problems and parent-teen conflict versus usual care in a randomised trial of 11-15-year-olds.
claims.source_title: Parent-teen behavior therapy + motivational interviewing for adolescents with ADHD
claims.authors_year: Sibley et al., 2016 (Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 84(8), 699-712)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: N = 128 adolescents aged 11-15 with ADHD, STAND versus treatment as usual; medium-to-large post-treatment effects on parent-rated symptoms, organisation/time management/planning, homework problems, parent-teen conflict and parenting stress; some effects diminished by 6-month follow-up; a later community-based effectiveness trial (Sibley et al., 2021, N about 278) found smaller effects that depended on therapist motivational-interviewing skill
claims.implication: Reframe the parent's role around the tracker: a fixed weekly parent-student meeting (the maths skill's Session C slot) where she chooses the week's goals and any privilege from a short menu, the dashboard is reviewed together, and the parent does not check work session by session. Avoid the 2 Sep pattern of a second full session the same day after problems; STAND-style monitoring is weekly and collaborative, not reactive.

claims.claim: Mastery experiences (actually succeeding at something that felt hard) are the strongest source of academic self-efficacy, ahead of encouragement, seeing others succeed, or feeling calm; praise only builds confidence when it is credible and backed by real success, so sequence work so she succeeds early in each session and ends on a success.
claims.source_title: Sources of Self-Efficacy in School: Critical Review of the Literature and Future Directions
claims.authors_year: Usher & Pajares, 2008 (Review of Educational Research, 78(4), 751-796); theory from Bandura, 1997, Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: critical review of studies measuring Bandura's four sources; mastery experience was the strongest and most consistent predictor of self-efficacy across school studies; social persuasion and physiological/affective states were weaker and less consistent
claims.implication: Keep the 10-minute retrieval starter as guaranteed early wins from secure topics, and require the exit ticket to end with one item at her secure level so every session closes on a success. The tracker already records mastery (topic promotions to secure, 'blanks per paper' falling); put that record where she sees it, since the brief says the Spanish chart is 'the reason she keeps playing'.

claims.claim: Visible small wins ('progress in meaningful work') were the single strongest predictor of a good day in a large diary study of knowledge workers, which supports showing the student what moved each session; but the evidence is correlational, from adults in workplaces, not from students or people with ADHD, so treat it as supporting C11 rather than as independent proof.
claims.authors_year: Amabile & Kramer, 2011 (Harvard Business Review, May 2011; book: The Progress Principle, 2011)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: 238 people in 26 project teams at 7 companies, about 12,000 daily diary entries; progress was reported on 76% of the best-mood days; setbacks had a larger negative effect than progress had a positive one
claims.implication: Consistent with the parent's stance (chart for progress, no streaks or obligation). A low-cost addition: a one-line 'what moved' summary after each logged session ('P1 now developing; 0 blanks; A4 sign check passed 4/5') on the student-facing view, and because setbacks weigh more than wins, never display a demotion as a headline.

claims.claim: Children with ADHD respond to reinforcement but need it more immediate, more frequent and more salient than typical children, and their performance drops under delayed or intermittent reward; so acknowledgement of an attempt must come in the same turn as the attempt, not at the end of the session or in the log.
claims.source_title: The impact of reinforcement contingencies on AD/HD: a review and theoretical appraisal
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: review of 22 experimental studies; children with ADHD showed stronger preference for immediate over delayed reward and greater performance deterioration under partial/delayed reinforcement than controls; both reward and response cost changed behaviour, with more consistent gains for immediate, continuous reinforcement
claims.implication: In maths-tutor-session, the labelled praise for attempting ('you wrote a first line, that is what gets method marks') must follow immediately when she writes anything after 'I can't'. Feedback on the exit ticket should be given item by item, not batched. The Shooting Gallery's immediate per-item feedback is already well matched to this and is probably part of why she keeps playing.

claims.claim: Behavioural approaches built on frequent labelled praise, planned ignoring of minor protest, and clear contingencies are the established psychosocial treatments for ADHD, but the adolescent evidence base is thinner than for children, and response cost (taking points or privileges away for errors or non-completion) is a punitive component that is easy to over-use and can escalate conflict, so positive contingencies should come first and losses, if used at all, must be small, pre-agreed and never for accuracy.
claims.source_title: Evidence-Based Psychosocial Treatments for Children and Adolescents With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
claims.authors_year: Evans, Owens, Wymbs & Ray, 2018 (Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology, 47(2), 157-198)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran); recalled, unverified: behavioural parent training, behavioural classroom management, behavioural peer interventions and organisation training rated well-established; combined training programmes for adolescents rated at a lower evidence level; response-cost evidence is mostly from elementary classrooms on on-task behaviour rather than learning outcomes
claims.implication: The tutor skill's scripted reply to 'I can't' ('what's one thing you could write down?') is planned ignoring done right: no debate, no long reassurance, redirect to a micro-step and praise the attempt. Keep the README's 'nothing is withheld for missing one' stance on evidence grounds, and if the parent ties home privileges to study, tie them to sessions attempted and questions submitted (Q4/Q5 were left unsubmitted), never to marks or accuracy.

caveats: PROVENANCE WARNING: the session's shared WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200 calls) before this agent's first search; all 13 planned searches were refused, and WebFetch/curl are blocked by egress policy. searches_run is therefore 0. Every URL above is a DOI or publisher URL recalled from memory, not a URL that appeared in a search result, and every figure in key_numbers is a recollection labelled 'unverified'. Verification agents should treat every claim as at best 'partial' until the source and numbers are confirmed, and any claim whose source cannot be found should be dropped from the report.

No ADHD-specific evidence on praise wording (C1-C3), feedback framing (C4-C5) or growth-mindset interventions (C6-C7) is cited; those claims are general-population and are applied to a 13-year-old with ADHD by inference. Whether the person-praise and inflated-praise effects are larger or smaller in ADHD is unknown to this agent.

The growth-mindset literature is actively contested: Sisk et al. 2018 and Macnamara & Burgoyne 2023 read the evidence as near-zero, Yeager et al. 2019 and Burnette et al. 2023 as small but real for targeted lower-achieving groups. The honest summary is 'small at best, near zero on average, cheap framing only'. No trial of mindset interventions specifically in ADHD samples is known to this agent.
C6 cites Sisk 2018 as its source but summarises Macnamara & Burgoyne 2023 and Burnette et al. 2023 from memory; the 2023 figures are the least certain numbers in this file.

STAND (C10) was delivered by trained therapists using motivational interviewing; the community-delivered replication showed smaller effects tied to therapist skill. A parent applying STAND-style principles via a skill file is a further step away from the trial conditions.

C12 (Amabile) is adult, correlational, workplace diary data; it is included because the brief asked for it, and is graded accordingly. It should not be used on its own to justify any dashboard feature.

C9 (RSD) rests on absence from DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 and the lack of a validated instrument; there may be 2023-2026 scoping or systematic reviews of RSD that this agent could not search for and that might refine the statement.

Response-cost evidence (C13, C14) is mostly from elementary-school classroom studies measuring on-task behaviour, not learning or exam outcomes in adolescents; the caution about escalation is an extrapolation shared by clinical reviews rather than a measured effect.
Emotion-dysregulation prevalence figures (C8) vary widely by definition and instrument; the ranges given are from memory of the review, not from a search summary.

The logged behaviours ('skip it', 'I can't', not showing working, answer-targeting) could reflect working-memory or executive-function load as much as emotion or motivation; the claims here do not distinguish those causes, and the sibling areas on executive function and cognitive load should be read alongside this one.

Nothing from 2023-2026 could be searched for; a re-run of this area with search budget available should look for: recent meta-analyses of feedback in one-to-one or AI tutoring, RSD scoping reviews, STAND follow-up trials, and any ADHD-specific praise or feedback studies.
